reason: The sources provide 18 highly detailed, cross-verified claims across multiple independent sites documenting the construction, navigation, and dramatic survival details of the voyage.
story: In 1915, pack ice crushed and sank Sir Ernest Shackleton's expedition ship, Endurance, leaving 28 men stranded on the freezing Antarctic ice. After escaping to bleak, uninhabited Elephant Island, Shackleton knew no rescue was coming. To save his crew, he and five men boarded the James Caird, a tiny 22-foot lifeboat modified by carpenter Harry McNish, who sealed its makeshift deck with seal blood. They faced the world's deadliest ocean, battling hurricane winds, freezing spray, and 40-foot waves. Navigator Frank Worsley guided them across 800 miles of stormy seas using just four fleeting sun sightings. After 17 grueling days, they reached South Georgia Island, but landed on the wrong side. Shackleton, Worsley, and Tom Crean then hiked 36 continuous hours across unmapped glaciers to reach a whaling station. Unbelievably, every single member of the 28-man crew survived.
angle: Navigator Frank Worsley guided a tiny 22-foot lifeboat across 800 miles of the world's most violent ocean using only four fleeting glimpses of the sun.

claims.claim: The expedition ship Endurance was trapped and crushed by pack ice in the Weddell Sea, eventually sinking.
The disaster left a total of 28 men stranded on the drifting Antarctic ice floes.
After the ice floes began breaking up in April 1916, the crew sailed in lifeboats to reach desolate Elephant Island.
Because Elephant Island was bleak and remote from shipping routes, Shackleton decided to sail to South Georgia to seek help.
The journey to South Georgia covered approximately 800 miles across the notoriously hostile Southern Ocean.
The journey was undertaken in the James Caird, a small lifeboat measuring between 22 and 23 feet long.
The lifeboat carried a crew of six men: Shackleton, Frank Worsley, Tom Crean, Harry McNish, John Vincent, and Timothy McCarthy.
Carpenter Harry McNish prepared the James Caird by raising its sides and building a makeshift wood and canvas deck.
McNish sealed the makeshift deck using a caulking mixture containing seal blood.
Shackleton confessed to navigator Frank Worsley shortly after setting sail that he actually knew nothing about sailing.
The crew's reindeer-hide sleeping bags shed hairs continuously, contaminating all of their food and drinks.
Worsley navigated the entire 800-mile journey using only four sun sightings, relying on dead reckoning for the rest.
Accumulating ice from freezing sea spray threatened to capsize the boat, forcing the crew to crawl onto the pitching deck to chip it away.
The grueling crossing of the Southern Ocean took 17 days to reach South Georgia.
After landing on South Georgia's uninhabited south coast, Shackleton, Worsley, and Crean crossed the unmapped mountainous interior on foot.
The three men completed the grueling, 36-hour continuous overland hike without a map to reach the Stromness whaling station.
Every single one of the 28 members of the Endurance crew ultimately survived the expedition.
The original James Caird lifeboat was returned to England and is now preserved on display at Dulwich College.

disputed: The exact length of the James Caird (Wikipedia and S4 state 22.5 feet, S2 and S7 state 22 feet, S6 states 23 feet). The script should refer to it generally as a '22-foot lifeboat'.
The exact distance of the voyage (S1 states 1,300 km or 700 nmi; S3 states 1,500 km or 800 nmi; S2, S4, S5, S6, S7 state 800 miles/nmi). The script should refer to the distance as '800 miles'.
The exact duration of the boat journey (S5 says 16 days, while S1, S4, and S6 state 17 days). The script should state '17 days' or 'over two weeks'.
